evidence.field: hanzi.etymology_notes[1]
evidence.text:
Simplified form of 學.  Originally composed of the numbers five (㐅) and six (六), representing study of arithmetic. 
Later two hands (又) were added on the left and right side of the character, possibly depicting counting with fingers or hands-on teaching.
Finally a child (子) was added to the bottom, depicting a child being educated.
The bottom part of 六 (six) was reanalyzed as 宀 (roof) and interpreted as a building for learning.

evidence.text:
Originally composed of the numbers five (㐅) and six (六), representing study of arithmetic. 
Later two hands (又) were added on the left and right side of the character, possibly depicting counting with fingers or hands-on teaching.

evidence.field: hanzi.etymology_notes[2]
evidence.text:
Possibly a phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *ɡruːɡ): phonetic 爻 (OC *ɢraːw) + phonetic 六 (OC *ruɡ). Later, 𦥑 was added to form 𦥯, and a semantic 子 (“child”) was added for differentiation.
Another explanation is abbreviated 敎 (“to teach”) + 𦥑 (“mingling hands; hands-on learning”) + 宀 (“house; roofed building”) – a child learning in a roofed place. However, the oracle bone script does not include a child.
In the modern form, 六 has corrupted to 冖 (“cover”), and the hands 𦥑 around the 爻 have become connected with the 冖. Shuowen regards 𦥑 as the phonetic component in the character, which may be true according to some Old Chinese reconstructions such as that of Pan Wuyun's, though probably not others.
See also the top component of 覺, which is a contraction of 學.
Endopassive/volitional derivation of 覺 (OC *kruːɡ, “to become aware”) (Sagart, 2004; Schuessler, 2007; Baxter and Sagart, 2014). Ultimately from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *kruk (“to rouse; to awaken; to disturb”).

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解；甲骨、金文、簡帛用例
evidence.text: The database reports oracle-bone forms of 學 and interprets them as hands manipulating counting or divination tallies, with 五 and 六 in some forms and 爻 in others. It proposes learning as the early sense, while also recording an alternative analysis in which 爻 is phonetic. The account says bronze forms add 子. It cites an oracle-bone occurrence in 《屯南》60, 于大學尋, and bronze occurrences including 大盂鼎’s 余唯即朕小學 and 靜簋’s learning/teaching archery passage. It also reports the Qin Shuihudi slip phrase 成學, “complete one’s studies,” and a Han-slip loan use of 學 for 覺, “feel/perceive.” These are source-reported readings and examples; the proposed tally interpretation is not uncontested.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 學

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解；甲骨文構形分析
evidence.text: The source describes 𦥑 as depicting two hands and identifies 五, 六, and sometimes 爻 in the oracle-bone graph. Separately, its 爻 entry reports oracle-bone use for divination, a separate possible depiction involving tally slips, and an oracle-bone use of 爻 read as 學 in a personal name. Thus, an early sound association between the graphs is reported, but this does not by itself establish that 爻 was a phonetic component in every form of 學. The source’s modern pronunciation display for 爻 offers yáo and xiáo readings; this is not ancient phonological evidence.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 學

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 《說文》 account and later usage chronology
evidence.text: The entry quotes the Shuowen account: 斆 is “to awaken/enlighten,” formed from 教 and 冖, with 𦥑 as phonetic; 學 is an abbreviated seal-script form of 斆. The entry also cites the Classic of Poetry line 日就月將，學有緝熙于光明, bronze-inscription uses for school and instruction, and the Qin slip 成學. It notes a Han-slip occurrence where 學 is read as 覺 in the sense “feel/perceive.” The attested extension from learning to school/instruction and the distinct Han loan spelling should be kept separate from the graphic-origin account.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 學

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解; competing construction account
evidence.text: The database also records a proposal attributed to Shirakawa Shizuka: 學 from 爻 and 宀, depicting crossed roof timbers and a school building. The database presents this as an alternative explanation, not its main analysis. The visible modern top ⺍/冖 should not be taken as direct evidence for a roof or building in the ancient graph; the oracle-bone and bronze forms are separately catalogued, and no glyph image was visually inspected for this report.

evidence.field: 學 headword entry; PDF p. 277, printed p. 265; scan-checked formation discussion and cited forms
evidence.text: The scan-verified entry, credited to 張標, presents multiple analyses of early 學 forms. It describes associative forms interpreted as 升 + 冖 or 林 + 冖; phonosemantic proposals involving 交 with 廾 or 冖, and 臼 with forms rendered as 両/丩; and says these structures began combining in Shang forms. It proposes that later Western Zhou forms added 子 to mark the child learner. It gives learning and imitation/efficacy as original senses and reports reciprocal 學/教 uses, including a Han use of 學 for huá as borrowing. These are this entry’s attributed proposals and reports, not an established consensus. SHA-256 of inspected scan: b058016d6914d7c19a11d120d8e37059bab845eb262c3b0312e478dbf7aa7836.

evidence.field: 學 headword; PDF p. 277, printed p. 265; scan pixels checked; continuation checked on PDF p. 278, printed p. 266
evidence.text: I inspected the supplied original scans. The 學 entry presents several attributed analyses: associative forms involving 升 with 冖 or 林 with 冖; a phonosemantic proposal in which 爻 supplies sound and 升 or 冖 is the other element; and a separate proposal using a rare element read jù, described as hands or claws, for sound and meaning. The scan says these structures began combining in Shang forms and proposes that 子 was added in Western Zhou forms to mark the child learner. It also reports learning and imitation/efficacy as original meanings and reciprocal 學/教 use. These are the book’s analyses and reports, not established consensus. In particular, the phrase 交织 (“interwoven”) describes 爻’s appearance; it is not a component identification as 交. The rare jù glyph remains scan-bound and is not assigned a guessed Unicode identity. Edition: 2012, ISBN 978-7-5528-0069-2; inspected scan SHA-256 PDF p. 277: b058016d6914d7c19a11d120d8e37059bab845eb262c3b0312e478dbf7aa7836; p. 278: 410c585d18389e14106c1eecf8438c3cce12d73ff11294f72c0d22cd3a722d02.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: The date of the cited oracle-bone occurrence 《屯南》60 was not independently established from an excavated-object catalogue in this pass; the source identifies it as an oracle-bone use, so it is reported as Shang-period evidence without a narrower date.

No glyph image was visually inspected. The positional graphic changes from oracle-bone to bronze, seal, clerical, and modern forms are summarized from the database’s text description and period labels only; no claim about a specific corruption pathway is made.

The early hands/tallies/counting interpretation and the 爻-as-phonetic possibility remain competing analyses. The alternate 爻+宀 school-building account is only attributed to Shirakawa in the consulted entry and was not independently corroborated with a primary publication.

The exact chronology of the extensions from learning to school, instruction/teaching, imitate/train, and knowledge is not fully established by a dated corpus here. Individual cited examples are separated by period, but they do not establish every semantic link or first occurrence.

The reported Han-slip use of 學 for 覺 is a graph-borrowing use distinct from graphic formation and from the character’s learning sense; no earlier occurrence or complete borrowing pathway was verified.

Unihan character-specific URLs for both 学 and 學 could not be opened. Local rows report current Mandarin xué for both, but the mandated official character-record click-through evidence could not be verified.

The supplied Baxter–Sagart row for 學 is MC haewk, OC *m-kˤruk. No corresponding local 爻 row was supplied, and the authors’ downloadable table failed to fetch; do not repeat a secondary transcription of 爻 as if cross-checked against the required local table.

No basis was found to treat the top of the modern simplified 学 as an ancient building/roof semantic component; its modern graphic relation to 學 is a standardized simplification, while detailed intermediate graphic changes remain unverified here.

The specific 《屯南》60 inscription’s archaeological date and context were not independently checked against an excavated-object catalogue; report only the source’s identification as oracle-bone evidence.

The hands/tally/counting analysis, possible 爻 phonetic role, and attributed 爻 + 宀 building analysis remain competing accounts. The latter was not independently checked against Shirakawa’s publication.
The cited period-separated examples do not establish a complete semantic chronology for learning, school, teaching, imitation, and knowledge, nor every link between those senses.
The Han-slip 學-for-覺 use is a reported graph borrowing distinct from graphic formation and ordinary learning use; no earlier borrowing occurrence or full phonological pathway was verified.
The exact Unihan pages for both 學 and 学 were inaccessible. Local kMandarin rows say xué, but the required official character-specific external click-through evidence is unavailable.
The local Baxter–Sagart table supplies 學 MC haewk and OC *m-kˤruk, but no local 爻 row; an independently checked same-system phonetic comparison is unavailable.
The Commons glyph is a modern vector tracing. Xiaoxuetang’s exact character result did not render in the web extraction, so no image-specific primary Xiaoxuetang record is proposed.

The supplied attachment may have been visually inspected in an earlier pipeline stage, but it was not independently displayed or inspected by the external web tool during this invocation. Commons metadata supports the modern-vector and CC0 descriptions only; it cannot substantiate a claim that this researcher visually inspected the rendered glyph.
The archaeological contexts and narrower dates of the named bronze-inscription examples were not independently checked in this focused review.
The image is a modern vector tracing; it should not be described as a photograph or direct scan of an excavated artifact.

The 《字源》 historical glyph sequence includes forms that are not safely represented by ordinary Unicode in the scan; this report paraphrases the textual component labels and does not assign identities to unresolved drawing variants.

The cited 《字源》 entries on printed pp. 264–265 were inspected in the supplied scan attachments. Edition metadata was checked against the existing local bibliography note, but a publisher-hosted full text or independent copy of the cited analysis was not accessible in this web pass.
